label: Armour models
description: How the unit absorbs damage. A card has one or two; a researched unit up to three. If more apply, first keep the models the unit has without any loadout pick; then keep the rarest (rare, then uncommon, then common; on a tie, the one listed first here). Name the others in armour.notes. Shields you switch on, barriers that protect allies, invulnerability and 'draw fire' are abilities, so they live in patterns instead. Code what this unit has. Protection that comes from where it stands (cover), from rank (veterancy), from an order every unit of its kind has (the retreat bonus) or from game settings (difficulty) is not a model, even though the unit benefits; mention it in armour.notes. A model built into the unit's own armour counts even when every unit of its kind in the game shares it (Company of Heroes rear armour). For a squad, code what protects each member; losing members is part of the squad crew model. A model that only an optional loadout pick gives (reactive armour, an auto-repair module, a shield item) still counts; say in armour.notes that it is a pick. Sensor traits differ: a sensor pick goes to sensors.notes, because a pick that changes how a unit is hit changes what beats it, while a sensor pick rarely does.

terms.label: Single health bar
terms.description: One health bar and nothing more: every hit just subtracts. The easiest to read.
examples: Red Alert 3: the Multigunner IFV has one health value; its armour type only scales the damage each kind of weapon does
Iron Harvest: fixed damage per armour class comes straight off health
terms.source_rule: Code it only when no other model on this list applies, and never together with another model. Damage scaled by armour type or class, as in most strategy games, is the armour class's job: it does not rule out flat-pool, and it does not make the unit another model.

terms.label: Directional armour
terms.description: The front is tougher than the sides and rear, so flanking pays off. Reads well from above if facing is obvious.
examples: Company of Heroes: rear hits multiply penetration
Broken Arrow: separate front, side, rear and top armour; tanks have almost none at the rear
PlanetSide 2: damage scales with the side the attacker stands on
Red Alert 3: mild; the tank armour sets take a little more damage on the sides and rear
Iron Harvest: many mechs take double damage from behind
terms.source_rule: Code it when the unit's own data, or a rule its game applies to every unit of its kind, makes side or rear hits do more, however little; say in armour.notes, in words, how much more. Leave it out when neither gives this unit facing values, even if some other units of its game have them.

terms.label: Penetration check
terms.description: Each hit is checked against the armour, and depending on angle or the weapon's penetration it may bounce for little or no damage.
examples: Company of Heroes: every hit rolls its penetration chance and bounces on a failure
Foxhole: hidden armour points; penetration chance rises as armour wears down
Wargame and Broken Arrow: weapons below the target's armour value do little or won't fire

terms.label: Zonal damage
terms.description: Parts such as tracks, turret, engine, rotor, legs or a weapon can be knocked out by damage before the unit dies, switching that function off for a while or for good. The part may be chosen by where the hit lands, by a heavy hit or by chance.
examples: MechWarrior and BattleTech: head, arm, leg and torso locations with their own armour
Foxhole: tracks, turret and fuel can be disabled by hits there
Company of Heroes: critical hits damage engines or kill gunners
Battlefield 4: a heavy hit can knock out a vehicle's movement, or a helicopter's control, for a few seconds
Wargame: critical hits on the crew disable specific systems
terms.source_rule: Code it when the sources say damage the unit takes can switch off one function (movement, steering, the turret or a weapon) while it lives on, however the part is chosen. A function lost because a crewman no player controls is hit (a gunner killed) counts too. A stun, root, slow or shutdown that comes from an enemy weapon's own effect is that weapon's trait or damage type, not zonal. Being disabled as a whole and burning at low health is critical-burn, not zonal.

terms.label: Crew casualties
terms.description: Hits can knock out seats: in a multi-seat vehicle a player can be ejected or killed while the vehicle survives.
examples: Foxhole: exposed seats leave their occupants open to fire
terms.source_rule: Code it only when hits can kill or throw out a player inside while the vehicle survives (open seats, shots through the glass). It needs two or more player seats, passenger seats included. Never for a squad: losing members is part of the squad crew model. A hit that only switches off a function by hurting a crewman no player controls is zonal.

terms.label: Recharging shield
terms.description: A shield layer over health soaks damage and recharges after a short pause without being hit.
examples: Halo: shields refill a few seconds after the last hit
StarCraft II: Protoss shields regenerate out of combat
PlanetSide 2: every soldier has a regenerating personal shield

terms.label: Charged shield
terms.description: A shield with its own charge that reduces incoming damage while it lasts; once drained, it has to be recharged with an item or at a station.
examples: ARC Raiders: light, medium and heavy shields take roughly half of each hit while charged; heavier ones slow you; refilled with recharger items or power cells from destroyed machines

terms.label: Ablative plates
terms.description: Armour plates soak hits and break off one by one, exposing the hull.
examples: Battlefield 3: reactive armour panels cancel the first anti-vehicle hit on each side
ARC Raiders: a heavy round can blow armour plates off a drone
BattleTech: bolt-on modular armour soaks damage first

terms.label: Damage reduction
terms.description: Armour takes a fixed amount off every hit, so small hits do little or nothing.
examples: StarCraft II: each unit's armour value comes off every hit; on the most armoured units, such as the Ultralisk or the Battlecruiser, a Marine's rifle loses a large part of each hit
terms.source_rule: Code it only when the game takes a fixed amount off each hit, and that amount changes which weapons work: the weapon of the game's basic rifle infantry loses a quarter or more of each hit to it. Judge the unit as bought, without upgrades. A smaller value only trims hits; mention it in armour.notes, in words. A cut by percentage or by damage type (guns doing half damage to tanks, small arms doing nothing to vehicles) belongs to the armour class and the damage map, not to this model.

terms.label: Self-repair
terms.description: Slowly regains health on its own, often only out of combat.
terms.notes: Passive. A heal on a key is the heal-self pattern; healing by dealing damage is the heal-on-hit weapon trait.
examples: PlanetSide 2: an auto-repair module heals vehicles out of combat
Battlefield 3: vehicles slowly regain armour

terms.label: Evasive
terms.description: Survives by dodging: the game gives it an explicit evasion mechanic (a dodge roll, a miss chance), not just a small size.
terms.source_rule: Code it only when the unit itself has a way to dodge: a dodge roll, a stated chance to avoid hits, or a hard-to-hit value of its own that is better than the game's basic rifle infantry has. Hit chance from cover, rank or moving, which every soldier of the game gets, is not evasive.

terms.label: Downed, revivable
terms.description: At zero health it goes down instead of dying: it can crawl, and a teammate can revive it or an enemy finish it.

terms.label: Weak point
terms.description: A small exposed spot, such as a vent, a joint or a fuel tank, takes extra damage when hit on purpose.
examples: ARC Raiders machines: shoot the joints and rear cylinders
terms.source_rule: Code it only for a spot the shooter must aim at. Extra damage to a whole side, the rear or the top is directional, even when the game calls it a weak spot.

terms.label: Interceptor
terms.description: An active protection system shoots down incoming missiles and rockets; it has few charges and must reload, so a volley can overwhelm it.
terms.notes: Automatic. Flares, chaff or smoke fired on a key to shake off missiles are the fire-countermeasures pattern.
examples: Broken Arrow: active protection stops HEAT rounds fully, kinetic ones partly, then reloads
Generals: the Paladin tank's point-defence laser shoots down incoming missiles
terms.source_rule: Code it only when the protection fires by itself. One the player switches on with a key, even for a few seconds, is the fire-countermeasures pattern.

terms.label: Critical burn
terms.description: Below a health threshold it is disabled and burning, and dies unless a teammate repairs it in time.
examples: Battlefield: vehicles below a threshold are disabled and burn out unless repaired
PlanetSide 2: vehicles catch fire at low health
Foxhole: many vehicles are disabled below a health threshold
